subjects.name: AQA Law
subjects.tagline: legal rules, evaluation, application and essay structure

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Criminal Law
notes: Criminal liability usually needs actus reus and mens rea to coincide.
Strong answers apply the offence elements to facts and evaluate possible defences.

topics.name: Tort Law
notes: Negligence answers should move through duty, breach, causation and remoteness.
Use case law to support each stage rather than naming cases without applying them.

topics.name: Legal System
notes: Legal system questions often reward clear institutional knowledge and balanced evaluation.
Examples strengthen evaluation of lay participation and access to justice.

topics.name: Law Making
notes: Law making requires process knowledge and criticism.
For interpretation, define the rule, explain its use, then evaluate certainty and fairness.

topics.name: Human Rights
notes: Human rights answers need article knowledge and proportionality reasoning.
Evaluation should consider the balance between individual liberty and public interest.

subjects.name: AQA Business
subjects.tagline: strategy, finance, marketing, operations and decision making

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Marketing
notes: Marketing answers should connect decisions to customer needs and competitive position.
Use context when judging whether a marketing strategy is suitable.

topics.name: Finance
notes: Finance questions often require calculation plus interpretation.
A strong conclusion links financial data to risk and objectives.

topics.name: Operations
notes: Operations decisions affect cost, quality, speed and flexibility.
Good evaluation considers trade-offs rather than pretending one method is always best.

topics.name: People Management
notes: People questions need theory applied to the business context.
Use evidence to judge the impact on productivity, retention and culture.

topics.name: Strategy
notes: Strategic answers should consider long-term direction and external pressure.
Evaluation should compare strategic options and justify a recommendation.

subjects.name: OCR Computer Science
subjects.tagline: systems, algorithms, programming and computational thinking

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year OCR figures

topics.name: Computer Architecture
notes: Architecture questions often test precise component roles.
Explain the process step-by-step, especially for CPU and memory operations.

topics.name: Networks
notes: Network answers need layered thinking and clear protocol roles.
Security questions should mention threats, prevention and limitations.

topics.name: Data Representation
notes: Show working in conversions and calculations.
For compression and encryption, compare method, purpose and trade-off.

topics.name: Algorithms
notes: Algorithm marks often come from dry-running and explaining efficiency.
Trace tables are a reliable way to prove you understand control flow.

topics.name: Programming
notes: Programming answers should use clear variables and structured logic.
State validation, testing and maintainability where relevant.

topics.name: Software Development
notes: Development questions reward comparison and project context.
Testing answers should include normal, boundary and erroneous data.

topics.name: Ethics and Legislation
notes: Ethics answers need both stakeholders and consequences.
Balance benefits against risks instead of writing one-sided opinions.

subjects.name: Edexcel Maths
subjects.tagline: pure maths, statistics, mechanics and problem solving

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year Edexcel figures

topics.name: Algebra
notes: Algebra is the language of the whole course.
Most mistakes come from weak manipulation rather than hard concepts.

topics.name: Calculus
notes: Calculus questions often combine method with interpretation.
Always check whether the answer requires exact form, units or a coordinate.

topics.name: Functions
notes: Function questions depend on notation and restrictions.
State domains carefully, especially for inverse functions.

topics.name: Trigonometry
notes: Trig requires both identity fluency and graph awareness.
Remember to find all solutions in the required interval.

topics.name: Sequences and Series
notes: Know when to use sequence formulae versus recurrence.
For binomial expansions, check validity conditions.

topics.name: Vectors
notes: Draw diagrams and define direction vectors clearly.
Use scalar product for angles and perpendicularity.

topics.name: Statistics
notes: Statistics answers need context, not just numbers.
Hypothesis tests require hypotheses, test statistic, conclusion and wording.

topics.name: Mechanics
notes: Mechanics rewards clear diagrams and sign conventions.
State assumptions when modelling real situations.

topics.name: Proof
notes: Proof is about logical explanation, not numerical evidence.
Use precise statements and avoid assuming the conclusion.

subjects.name: AQA Psychology
subjects.tagline: approaches, research methods, biopsychology and evaluation

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Social Influence
notes: Use studies and evaluation together, not separately.
Application questions often ask you to identify processes in a scenario.

topics.name: Memory
notes: Memory essays should explain models before evaluating evidence.
EWT questions need careful attention to cognitive interview detail.

topics.name: Attachment
notes: Attachment topics reward precise study detail and ethical evaluation.
Distinguish deprivation from privation clearly.

topics.name: Psychopathology
notes: Link explanations to treatments where possible.
Evaluation should compare biological and psychological approaches.

topics.name: Approaches
notes: Approaches questions often ask for assumptions and evaluation.
Use comparisons to show depth.

topics.name: Biopsychology
notes: Biopsychology needs accurate biological terminology.
Diagrams can help organise processes like synaptic transmission.

topics.name: Research Methods
notes: Research methods marks are often practical and procedural.
Always explain how a design choice affects validity or reliability.

topics.name: Issues and Debates
notes: Issues and debates can be applied across the entire course.
Use examples from named topics to avoid generic evaluation.

subjects.name: AQA Sociology
subjects.tagline: theories, methods, education, families, crime and beliefs

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Education
notes: Education essays need evidence from internal and external factors.
Always link sociologists to the question focus.

topics.name: Methods
notes: Methods answers need strengths, limitations and context.
Applied methods should connect the method to the research group.

topics.name: Theory
notes: Theory is strongest when applied to social issues.
Compare perspectives directly rather than listing them.

topics.name: Families and Households
notes: Family essays reward trends, evidence and theoretical debate.
Use contemporary examples for diversity and changing roles.

topics.name: Beliefs in Society
notes: Beliefs questions often hinge on evidence for or against secularisation.
Use global examples where appropriate.

topics.name: Crime and Deviance
notes: Crime essays need theory, evidence and evaluation.
Distinguish explanations of offending from explanations of social construction.

subjects.name: WJEC Criminology
subjects.tagline: crime theories, campaigns, justice and controlled assessment skills

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year WJEC figures

topics.name: Types of Crime
notes: Crime type answers need examples and reasons for under-reporting.
Distinguish legal categories from social perceptions.

topics.name: Campaigns for Change
notes: Campaign work needs clear aims, target audience and methods.
Evaluation should measure whether the campaign could change awareness or law.

topics.name: Media Representation
notes: Media questions ask how crime is portrayed and why.
Use examples to support claims about fear or distortion.

topics.name: Criminological Theories
notes: Theory answers need explanation, evidence and criticism.
Compare theories by how well they explain different crimes.

topics.name: Crime Scene to Courtroom
notes: Investigation answers should follow the process from scene to charge.
Mention reliability and limitations of evidence.

topics.name: Courtroom Process
notes: Courtroom questions need roles and process knowledge.
Evaluation can consider fairness, bias and effectiveness.

topics.name: Justice System
notes: Justice system answers need agency roles and relationships.
Use examples of formal and informal social control.

topics.name: Punishment
notes: Punishment essays should compare aims and effectiveness.
Use recidivism, cost and ethics in evaluation.

channels.name: Criminology Web
channels.note: topic walkthroughs and controlled assessment support

subjects.name: Edexcel Geography
subjects.tagline: physical systems, human systems, synoptic thinking and fieldwork

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year Edexcel figures

topics.name: Tectonics
notes: Tectonics answers need process knowledge and place evidence.
Evaluate risk using governance, development and vulnerability.

topics.name: Coasts
notes: Coasts questions need landform processes and systems thinking.
Use case studies when judging management.

topics.name: Water and Carbon Cycles
notes: Cycle questions require systems vocabulary.
Link human activity to changing stores and flows.

topics.name: Globalisation
notes: Globalisation answers need winners, losers and scale.
Use named examples for flows and impacts.

topics.name: Regeneration
notes: Regeneration needs place-specific evidence.
Evaluation should consider different stakeholders.

topics.name: Superpowers
notes: Superpower questions ask about hard, soft and smart power.
Use current geopolitical examples carefully.

topics.name: Migration
notes: Migration questions need causes, impacts and policy responses.
Balance economic, social and political dimensions.

topics.name: Fieldwork and NEA
notes: Fieldwork marks come from method justification and evaluation.
Be precise about limitations and improvements.

topics.name: Synoptic Links
notes: Synoptic answers connect multiple parts of the course.
Use evidence from resources and your own knowledge.

subjects.name: AQA Biology
subjects.tagline: cells, biochemistry, genetics, ecology and practical analysis

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Biological Molecules
notes: Molecule questions need structure-function links.
Enzyme questions often require graph interpretation and controls.

topics.name: Cells
notes: Cells topics reward precise terminology and process order.
Use magnification formulae carefully.

topics.name: Exchange and Transport
notes: Exchange answers should connect structure to efficient transport.
Use pressure gradients and surface area where relevant.

topics.name: Energy Transfers
notes: Energy pathways require sequence and location knowledge.
Do not confuse reduced NADP with reduced NAD.

topics.name: Responses
notes: Responses questions often test coordination and negative feedback.
Use named hormones and effectors accurately.

topics.name: Genetics and Populations
notes: Genetics requires careful notation and probability reasoning.
Population genetics questions need assumptions and interpretation.

topics.name: Ecology
notes: Ecology answers need interactions between biotic and abiotic factors.
Use data to support conclusions.

topics.name: Required Practicals
notes: Practical questions reward method logic and error awareness.
State control variables and justify improvements.

subjects.name: AQA English Literature
subjects.tagline: texts, contexts, interpretations and essay arguments

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year AQA figures

topics.name: Shakespeare
notes: Shakespeare essays need close method analysis and dramatic purpose.
Use context to illuminate meaning rather than bolt it on.

topics.name: Poetry
notes: Poetry answers should analyse form and structure as well as language.
Comparisons work best around argument, not feature spotting.

topics.name: Prose
notes: Prose essays need a clear line of argument.
Embed quotations and explore alternative interpretations.

topics.name: Modern Texts
notes: Modern text essays often reward social and historical context.
Discuss writer's methods and wider meanings together.

topics.name: Context
notes: Context should support interpretation, not replace analysis.
Use precise context rather than generic background.

topics.name: Comparison
notes: Comparison requires an argument that holds both texts together.
Avoid alternating paragraphs with no synthesis.

topics.name: Critical Views
notes: Critical views should challenge or extend your argument.
Use critics briefly and purposefully.

channels.name: Mr Bruff
channels.note: English literature analysis and exam skills

subjects.name: OCR English Literature
subjects.tagline: drama, poetry, prose, comparison and critical readings

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year OCR figures

topics.name: Drama
notes: Drama answers should discuss performance and audience effect.
Analyse structure, stage directions and dramatic tension.

topics.name: Poetry
notes: Poetry needs close analysis of language and pattern.
Use technical vocabulary only when it supports meaning.

topics.name: Prose
notes: Prose responses need argument and textual detail.
Consider narrative perspective and structural choices.

topics.name: Comparison
notes: Comparison should be conceptual, not just text-by-text.
Write around themes and methods across both texts.

topics.name: Context
notes: OCR rewards contextual awareness when it shapes interpretation.
Avoid generic context that could apply to any text.

topics.name: Critical Interpretations
notes: Critical readings should be integrated into your argument.
Use critics to create debate, not decoration.

subjects.name: Edexcel History
subjects.tagline: source analysis, interpretations, depth studies and coursework

papers.name: Themes in Breadth with Aspects in Depth

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year Edexcel figures

topics.name: Breadth Study
notes: Breadth essays need long-term patterns.
Use chronology to show change over time.

topics.name: Depth Study
notes: Depth essays need precise evidence and explanation.
Avoid narrative by linking facts to the question.

topics.name: Themes
notes: Thematic essays need connections across periods.
Structure around argument, not chronology alone.

topics.name: Source Skills
notes: Source answers should use content and provenance together.
Evaluate utility for the specific enquiry.

topics.name: Interpretations
notes: Interpretations questions need comparison of views.
Explain why historians may differ.

topics.name: Coursework
notes: Coursework needs a focused question and sustained judgement.
Use historians critically rather than descriptively.

topics.name: Essay Skills
notes: Strong history essays use criteria to judge importance.
Every paragraph should advance the argument.

subjects.name: Edexcel Politics
subjects.tagline: UK politics, government, political ideas and comparative politics

boundaries.source: Starter boundary model - replace with official last-year Edexcel figures

topics.name: Democracy and Participation
notes: Democracy essays need examples and balanced judgement.
Use turnout, participation and pressure group evidence.

topics.name: Political Parties
notes: Party questions need ideology, policy and electoral evidence.
Compare parties directly where possible.

topics.name: Elections and Voting
notes: Elections answers should use data and examples.
Evaluate electoral systems by representation, stability and accountability.

topics.name: Political Ideas
notes: Ideology essays need core ideas and thinkers.
Use strands within ideologies to create debate.

topics.name: Constitution
notes: Constitution answers need principles and reform examples.
Evaluate whether change has gone too far or not far enough.

topics.name: Parliament
notes: Parliament questions should assess effectiveness, not just describe roles.
Use examples of scrutiny and rebellion.

topics.name: Prime Minister and Executive
notes: Executive essays need power versus constraint.
Use examples of leadership style and events.

topics.name: Judiciary
notes: Judiciary answers should distinguish independence and neutrality.
Use case examples to support evaluation.

topics.name: US Politics
notes: US politics needs institutional knowledge and examples.
Comparisons should be explicit and criteria-based.

topics.name: Comparative Theories
notes: Comparative theories explain why systems differ.
Apply theories rather than naming them at the end.
